title: Evaluating Statistical Claims
subtitle: Identify bias, generalizability, and the difference between correlation and causation

sections.title: The Two Big Questions
sections.content:
Every statistical claim question on the SAT asks one of two things:

1. **Is the sample biased?** Does it represent the population fairly?
2. **How broadly can we generalize?** Who does the conclusion actually apply to?

A secondary question:
3. **Causation vs. correlation:** Can the study conclude that one thing *causes* another?

sections.title: What Makes a Sample Biased?
sections.content:
A sample is **biased** when it systematically over-represents or under-represents part of the population.

**Biased sampling methods:**
- Surveying only people who already agree with the hypothesis
- Asking only one subgroup (dog owners about a dog park)
- Voluntary response (people with strong opinions respond more)
- Convenience sampling (only surveying easily accessible people)

**Unbiased:** random sampling from the full population

sections.title: Example: Dog Park Survey
sections.problem: A city council surveyed 500 **dog owners** about converting a field to a dog park. The majority said yes. Which is the best description of the survey's limitation?

steps.description: The council wants to know all residents' opinions, but only surveyed dog owners
Dog owners have a systematic reason to favor a dog park — this is bias
steps.math: \text{Sample is biased: not representative of all residents}

sections.answer: The survey sample is **biased** because it only includes dog owners, who are more likely to support a dog park than the general population.
sections.tip: Bias means the sample is not representative of the target population — certain groups are over- or under-represented.

sections.title: Type 2: Identifying the Target Population for Generalization
Conclusions Apply Only to the Population Sampled
sections.content:
The conclusions from a study can only be extended to the **largest population** that the sample fairly represents.

**Rules:**
- If you randomly sampled California State University history professors → can generalize to *all California State University history professors*
- Cannot generalize to all U.S. professors, or all history professors nationwide
- Cannot generalize beyond the sampling frame

sections.title: Example: Scope of Generalization
sections.problem: Researchers randomly selected history professors from the California State Universities and asked about textbook publishers. What is the largest population this generalizes to?

steps.description: Random sample: only from California State Universities
The sample represents only this specific population
steps.math: \text{Largest valid population: all history professors at all California State Universities}

sections.answer: All **history professors at all California State Universities**

sections.title: Example: School-Level vs. District-Level
sections.problem: 40 fourth-grade students were randomly selected from a certain school. 32 thought the morning announcements were helpful. What is the largest population this generalizes to?

steps.description: The sample was from one school, fourth-grade specifically
steps.math: \text{Sampling frame: fourth-graders at this specific school}

steps.description: Cannot generalize to other schools or all grade levels
steps.math: \text{Largest valid: all fourth-grade students at the school}

sections.answer: All **fourth-grade students at that specific school**

sections.title: Type 3: What CAN Be Concluded from a Random Sample
Example: Correct Conclusion from a Random Sample
sections.problem:
1,000 adults were randomly selected from a large city. 78% said they're satisfied with air quality. Which statements can be concluded?

I. About 78% of all city residents are satisfied with air quality.
II. The sampling method produces reliable estimates.

steps.description: Because the sample was random and large, it is representative
steps.math: \text{Statement I: can be inferred — random sample from the city} \checkmark

steps.description: Random sampling is a reliable method

sections.answer: Both Statement I and Statement II can be concluded.
sections.tip: A **random** sample allows generalization to the population it was drawn from. Non-random samples do not.

sections.title: Observational vs. Experimental Studies
sections.content:
- **Observational study:** researchers observe without intervening. Can only show **correlation** (association), not causation.
- **Randomized experiment:** subjects are randomly assigned to treatment or control groups. When done correctly, can show **causation**.

Key rule:
- If researchers did NOT randomly assign subjects to groups → cannot conclude causation → observational study
- If researchers DID randomly assign → can conclude causation → experiment

sections.title: Example: Can We Conclude Causation?
sections.problem: A psychologist chose 35 students at random from one middle school. Half were randomly assigned to play an educational game; the other half didn't. Those who played the game had higher accuracy on fraction problems. Can the psychologist conclude the game *caused* improved accuracy?

steps.description: Were subjects randomly assigned to groups? YES — half were randomly assigned to play the game
Random assignment means the groups were initially similar in all ways, so differences in outcome are due to the treatment
But: sample was from one school — generalization is limited to students like those
steps.math: \text{Can generalize only to students at that school (or similar middle school students)}

sections.answer: Yes, causation can be concluded for the students in the study. But results generalize only to students similar to those in the sample.

sections.title: Key Takeaways
items: **Biased sample:** only represents part of the population → conclusions don't generalize well
**Random sample:** can generalize to the population it was drawn from, but no further
**Generalization scope:** limited to the sampling frame — the specific group from which the sample was drawn
**Correlation ≠ causation:** observational studies can show association; only randomized experiments can show causation
**Random assignment (experiment):** allows causal conclusions within the study population

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- Generalizing to a larger population than was sampled (e.g., all U.S. students from one school's sample)
- Concluding causation from an observational study
- Saying a biased sample produces NO useful information — it still shows what's true for the biased group
- Confusing 'random sample' (who is selected) with 'random assignment' (how subjects are divided into groups)

sat_tips: Ask: 'Who was sampled?' — conclusions only apply to that group
Ask: 'Were subjects randomly assigned to treatment groups?' — if yes, causation is possible
Biased sample ≠ no information, just limited generalizability
The 'largest population' question: always limit to the actual sampling frame (the group actually sampled from)
